newsitem.title: USA: US prosecutors charge 18 with securities fraud.
newsitem.headline: US prosecutors charge 18 with securities fraud.

text.p: Federal prosecutors said on Wednesday they charged a group of 18 persons with securities fraud for using high-pressure sales tactics and issuing false data to boost the stock price of a bogus Internet company.

The fraud involved mostly Russian immigrants, who schemed to inflate the price of Globus Group Inc from 25 cents to $8.00 a share between January and September last year, illegally netting about $8.0 million, they said.
When the ring stopped pitching the stock in October, its price fell to less than $0.40, leaving some 800 mostly elderly investors millions of dollars in losses, the prosecutors said.

Each defendant faces more than 100 years behind bars if convicted. The 22-count indictment also includes mail and wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, illegal phone solicitation and counts of murder for hire.

The group allegedly set up Globus as a shell corporation and toted it as an Internet service provider that linked importers and exporters. Globus then opened offshore companies in Antigua, West Indies and in Nassau, Bahamas to which it funnelled money raised from U.S. investors. The money later ended up in the pockets of the defendants, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors identified the head of the ring as Alexander Shindman, 30, who was arrested Wednesday morning at his Boca Raton, Fla., home.

"In the past few years stock fraud schemes of the sort charged in this indictment have become a new form of organized crime," said Zachary Carter, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District in Brooklyn that is prosecuting the case.
At least four of the defendants are still at large. The others were were arrested by agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation at their homes in Brooklyn, New Jersey and Florida.
Their arrest capped an 11-month investigation by the FBI and federal securities regulators.

The defendants allegedly solicited investors though cold telephone calls from a company called Hillcrest Financial Corp in Manhattan. Sales were processed through Bear Stearns, which was not charged in the case.

Some of the false information the group gave investors included one claiming Globus had won a $12 million lawsuit from AT&T Corp and another saying Globus was investing $3.9 million in a company called the Kingston Operating Corp. The company also issued false press releases.

Two members of the group, Igor Stolyar, 27, and his father, Alix Stolyar, 48, both of Brooklyn, where also charged with arranging to hire a hit man in Canada to kill two men who were supposedly shaking them down. The murders were never carried out.
Prosecutors did not link the case with organized crime involving the Russian Mafia, which operate in Brooklyn.
